summary.text: In the prime case, \(\varphi(m)\ge 2^N\) together with \(\varphi(m)\le m-1\) makes the Fermat number the least possible candidate. In the composite case, any smaller candidate would have \(\varphi(m)=2^N\); writing \(m=2^c k\) with \(k\) odd shows that \(k\) is squarefree with all prime factors among Fermat numbers of index below \(33\), so \(k\le\prod_{i<33}F_i=2^N-1\), while multiplicativity of the totient then forces \(m\ge2^{N+1}\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F_i=2^{2^i}+1.
\]
Thus in particular
\[
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1.
\]
For a nonnegative integer \(n\), define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid\varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

We first record the elementary facts about Euler's totient and Fermat numbers that will be used.

For every integer \(m>1\),
\[
\varphi(m)\le m-1.
\]
Moreover, if
\[
m=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p}
\]
is its prime factorization, then
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}p^{e_p-1}(p-1). \tag{1}
\]
Consequently, for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), the number \(p-1\) divides \(\varphi(m)\).

We will also use the Fermat-number product identity
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}F_i=F_r-2=2^{2^r}-1. \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, this follows by induction. For \(r=0\), the empty product is \(1=F_0-2\). If the formula holds for \(r\), put \(x=2^{2^r}\), so that \(F_r=x+1\). Then
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{r}F_i=(F_r-2)F_r=(x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1
=2^{2^{r+1}}-1=F_{r+1}-2.
\]

We next establish two lower-bound principles.

First, suppose that \(M>0\), \(m>0\), and \(2^M\mid\varphi(m)\). Since \(2^M>1\), we cannot have \(m=1\), because \(\varphi(1)=1\). Hence \(m>1\). Positivity of \(\varphi(m)\), together with the divisibility, gives
\[
2^M\le \varphi(m)\le m-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
m\ge 2^M+1. \tag{3}
\]

The second lower bound is more specialized. Suppose that \(M>0\),
\[
\varphi(m)=2^M,
\]
and write
\[
m=2^c k
\]
with \(k\) odd. Assume also that
\[
k\le 2^M-1. \tag{4}
\]
We claim that
\[
m\ge 2^{M+1}. \tag{5}
\]

Because \(k\) is odd, \(2^c\) and \(k\) are coprime, so the totient is multiplicative across these two factors:
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(2^c)\varphi(k). \tag{6}
\]
If \(k=1\), then \(m=2^c\). The case \(c=0\) would give \(\varphi(m)=1\), contrary to \(M>0\). Thus \(c>0\), and
\[
2^M=\varphi(2^c)=2^{c-1}.
\]
Hence \(c=M+1\), so in this case \(m=2^{M+1}\).

Now suppose \(k>1\). We first show that \(c>0\). If \(c=0\), then \(m=k\) and
\[
2^M=\varphi(k)\le k-1.
\]
But (4) gives \(k-1<2^M\), a contradiction. Thus \(c>0\). Using \(\varphi(2^c)=2^{c-1}\), equation (6) becomes
\[
2^{c-1}\varphi(k)=2^M. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(m=2^c k\), multiplying appropriately gives
\[
m\varphi(k)=2^c k\varphi(k)=2^{M+1}k. \tag{8}
\]
Because \(k>1\), one has \(0<\varphi(k)<k\). Therefore
\[
2^{M+1}\varphi(k)<2^{M+1}k=m\varphi(k).
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(\varphi(k)\) yields \(2^{M+1}<m\). This proves (5) in all cases.

We now treat the two alternatives concerning \(F_{33}\).

Assume first that \(F_{33}\) is prime. Since
\[
F_{33}=2^N+1,
\]
we have
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^N.
\]
Thus \(F_{33}\) is an admissible integer in the definition of \(a(N)\). On the other hand, (3), applied with \(M=N\), says that every admissible positive integer \(m\) satisfies
\[
m\ge 2^N+1=F_{33}.
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
a(N)=F_{33}
\]
when \(F_{33}\) is prime.

It remains to prove the other branch. Assume henceforth that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. The integer
\[
2^{N+1}
\]
is admissible, because
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N.
\]
Thus it is enough to prove that no smaller positive integer is admissible.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that
\[
0<m<2^{N+1},\qquad 2^N\mid\varphi(m). \tag{9}
\]
We first show that divisibility in (9) is actually equality:
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N. \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, \(\varphi(m)>0\), so \(\varphi(m)=q2^N\) for some positive integer \(q\). Also \(m\ne1\), since \(2^N>1\) does not divide \(\varphi(1)=1\). Hence
\[
\varphi(m)<m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot 2^N.
\]
It follows that \(q<2\), and positivity forces \(q=1\), proving (10).

Write the unique decomposition of \(m\) into its power-of-two and odd parts as
\[
m=2^c k,\qquad k\text{ odd}. \tag{11}
\]
Our next goal is to prove the crucial bound
\[
k\le 2^N-1. \tag{12}
\]

Because \(2^c\) and \(k\) are coprime, equations (10) and (11) imply
\[
\varphi(2^c)\varphi(k)=2^N.
\]
In particular, \(\varphi(k)\) divides \(2^N\). Every positive divisor of a power of \(2\) is itself a power of \(2\), so for some \(T\le N\),
\[
\varphi(k)=2^T. \tag{13}
\]

We claim first that \(k\) is squarefree. Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(k\), and let its exponent in \(k\) be \(e\). Formula (1), applied to \(k\), shows that the factor
\[
p^{e-1}(p-1)
\]
divides \(\varphi(k)=2^T\). If \(e\ge2\), then the odd prime \(p\) divides \(2^T\), which is impossible. Thus \(e=1\) for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(k\), and hence
\[
k=\prod_{p\mid k}p, \tag{14}
\]
where the product runs over distinct primes.

We next determine the possible form of each such odd prime \(p\). Since \(p\mid k\mid m\), formula (1), now applied to \(m\), shows that
\[
p-1\mid\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]
Therefore
\[
p-1=2^a
\]
for some \(a\le N\), and hence
\[
p=2^a+1. \tag{15}
\]
Since \(p\) is an odd prime, \(p\ne2\), so \(a\ne0\).

If \(2^a+1\) is prime and \(a>0\), then \(a\) must itself be a power of \(2\). To see this directly, write
\[
a=2^i d
\]
where \(d\) is odd. If \(d>1\), set \(x=2^{2^i}>1\). Then
\[
2^a+1=x^d+1
\]
is divisible by \(x+1\), since \(d\) is odd; and because \(d>1\), this is a proper nontrivial factorization. That contradicts primality. Thus \(d=1\), so \(a=2^i\). Equation (15) therefore gives
\[
p=2^{2^i}+1=F_i \tag{16}
\]
for some \(i\ge0\). In other words, every prime divisor of the odd part \(k\) is a Fermat number which is itself prime.

We now show that the index \(i\) in (16) must satisfy
\[
i<33. \tag{17}
\]
It cannot equal \(33\), because then \(p=F_{33}\) would be prime, contrary to our present assumption.

If instead \(i\ge34\), the Fermat numbers increase with their index, so
\[
p=F_i\ge F_{34}=2^{2^{34}}+1.
\]
Since \(N=2^{33}\), we have
\[
N+1=2^{33}+1\le 2^{34}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{N+1}\le 2^{2^{34}}<F_{34}\le p. \tag{18}
\]
But \(p\mid m\) and \(m>0\), so \(p\le m\). This contradicts \(m<2^{N+1}\) from (9). Thus neither \(i=33\) nor \(i\ge34\) is possible, and (17) follows.

By (14), the odd number \(k\) is a product of distinct prime divisors. By (16) and (17), these divisors form a subset of
\[
F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_{32}.
\]
All these factors exceed \(1\), so the product over any subset is at most the product over the full set. Using the Fermat product identity (2), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
k
&\le \prod_{i=0}^{32}F_i\\
&=F_{33}-2\\
&=2^{2^{33}}-1\\
&=2^N-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (12).

We may now apply the second lower-bound principle to (10), (11), and (12), with \(M=N\). Notice that \(N=2^{33}>0\). It gives
\[
m\ge2^{N+1},
\]
contradicting the strict inequality in (9). Therefore there is no positive admissible \(m<2^{N+1}\).

Since \(2^{N+1}\) itself is admissible and every admissible positive integer is at least this large, we conclude that when \(F_{33}\) is not prime,
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}.
\]

Recalling that \(N=2^{33}\), the two cases together give
\[
\boxed{
 a(2^{33})=
 \begin{cases}
 F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1,&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
 2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}}
\]
